# Lexoral

> Lexoral is an independent Canadian provider of bilingual French–English legal transcription, based in Kanata (Ottawa), Ontario, serving Canada and the United States. It produces verbatim, line-numbered, court-ready transcripts of depositions, examinations, arbitrations, tribunal hearings, criminal proceedings and recorded evidence, each with a signed accuracy declaration from the named practitioner who produced it, and Loi 25-compliant file handling.

Coverage: entirely American files, entirely Canadian files, or both at once. Work is produced from the recording, so recordings are accepted from any jurisdiction; remote intake, no travel charge.

Proceedings transcribed:
- United States: depositions, examinations before trial, examinations under oath (EUO), arbitration hearings, recorded statements, 911 and emergency-services calls, custodial and police-station interviews, body-worn and covert recordings, wiretap and consensual recordings.
- Canada: examinations for discovery, interrogatoires hors cour, out-of-court examinations, criminal trials and preliminary inquiries, labour and grievance arbitration, administrative tribunals, professional discipline councils, coroner's inquests, immigration hearings, commissions of inquiry.
- Cross-border: a Canadian witness examined for a U.S. matter, a U.S. party filing in Quebec, parallel proceedings, cross-border arbitration, letters rogatory and Hague Evidence Convention examinations.

Areas served: Montréal, Québec, Laval, Longueuil, Gatineau, Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivières, Ottawa, Kanata, Toronto, Moncton, Winnipeg, New York, Boston, Buffalo, Detroit, Chicago, Burlington, Portland, Seattle, Los Angeles, Miami.

Three situations where the work matters:

1. Genuinely bilingual proceedings, where both languages are the record. Criminal matters under a section 530 order; Quebec examinations and trials under section 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867; Ontario bilingual proceedings under section 126 of the Courts of Justice Act; Federal Court, Tax Court and courts martial under Part III of the Official Languages Act; New Brunswick, where both languages are official in the courts. Section 530.1(g) of the Criminal Code requires the record to contain a transcript of everything said in the official language it was said in, a transcript of any interpretation into the other, and documentary evidence in the language it was tendered.

2. Recorded evidence in French, where no reporter was ever present. 911 and emergency-services calls, custodial and police-station interviews, wiretap and consensual recordings, body-worn and covert recordings, voicemail and recorded telephone calls, recorded meetings and interviews. Where the evidence is a foreign-language recording, U.S. federal practice treats the English transcript as the evidence rather than as an aid, and where accuracy is disputed each side may put its own translation before the jury (Ninth Circuit Model Criminal Jury Instruction 2.8). In United States v. Chavez, 976 F.3d 1178 (10th Cir. 2020), the court held that "English-translation transcripts may be admitted only in addition to the underlying foreign-language recordings, not in lieu of them", and that admitting the transcripts without the recordings violated the best-evidence rule and was reversible error.

3. Interpreted proceedings where accuracy is already in issue: errata under Rule 30(e), motions to correct, competing transcripts, cross-examination of an interpreter, appeal. Stated honestly: in most U.S. circuits the interpreter's English is attributed to the witness under the language-conduit rule, and this work is not worth buying unless accuracy is genuinely in issue.

Why a bilingual reporter is not optional: in R. v. Munkonda, 2015 ONCA 309, the Court of Appeal for Ontario quashed a committal for trial after a bilingual preliminary inquiry; among the breaches identified was that the court reporter was not bilingual. In Quebec, stenographer accreditation is granted per language: under the Regulation respecting the training, skill and knowledge evaluation, accreditation and discipline of stenographers, CQLR c. B-1, r. 13, s. 1, "the accreditation is valid for the methods and languages indicated thereon", and the Barreau du Québec's published roll carries a language column for that reason.

Every transcript: verbatim with each language transcribed as spoken; continuous line numbering and structured pagination; speaker identification and objection notation; timestamps at speaker changes; conventions page; signed accuracy declaration from the named practitioner; searchable PDF and editable Word; five business days.

On request: forty-eight hour priority; condensed (four-up) and word index; original language and interpretation in parallel; line-matched comparison against an official transcript; rough draft before certification; ASCII, e-transcript and RTF; exhibit scanning and hyperlinking; produced to a named forum's own conventions.

Key facts:
- Two named practitioners (Brian Fino, Raymond Carby-Samuels). No contractor pool, no offshore desk, no model output presented as reviewed. The accuracy declaration is signed by the person who did the work.
- The practitioner who transcribes French legal argument is a jurist: former Quebec paralegal and active Associate Member of the Canadian Bar Association, author and publisher of constitutional framework and civil liberties textbooks in English and French, has delivered complex legal argument in French before Quebec's National Assembly, and lectures in Canadian constitutional law and human rights codes at George Brown College.
- Pricing: per page, quoted in Canadian dollars after audio review. Confirmation the same working day.
- Privacy: Loi 25 and GDPR compliant; encrypted transfer; client materials never used for AI training or any external purpose; permanent deletion on request.
- Clients: litigation firms, arbitration panels (ICC, AAA, ICDR, ADRIC, CIAC), government and administrative tribunals, in-house legal departments, insurance defence, public defence and legal aid, academic research.
- Contact: secure@lexoral.org (files and proceedings), contact@lexoral.org (everything else), +1 (514) 712-7516 (also WhatsApp).
- Address: 24191-300 Eagleson Rd, Kanata, ON K2M 2C3, Canada.

## Pages

- [Home (English)](https://lexoral.org/): coverage, where the work matters, services, cross-border comparison, the record, contact.
- [Accueil (français)](https://lexoral.org/fr/): version française de la page d'accueil.
- [Legal transcription in Quebec](https://lexoral.org/quebec/): section 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867 makes either language usable by any person in the courts of Quebec, so both languages are the record and no interpreter is involved; what a bilingual examination looks like minute by minute; per-language stenographer accreditation under CQLR c. B-1, r. 13; procedures transcribed; cities served (Montreal, Quebec City, Laval, Gatineau, Longueuil, Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivières, Saguenay, Lévis). States plainly that Lexoral is not an accredited Quebec official stenographer.
- [Transcription juridique au Québec](https://lexoral.org/quebec-fr/): version française.
- [French recordings as evidence](https://lexoral.org/recorded-evidence/): forensic transcription and transcription-translation of French-language recorded evidence; the recording is the evidence and the transcript assists (United States v. Chavez, 976 F.3d 1178 (10th Cir. 2020)); source-language transcription produced first and the translation aligned to it line by line, per NAJIT's Position Paper: General Guidelines and Requirements for Transcription Translation in a Legal Setting (May 2019); Taniguchi v. Kan Pacific Saipan, 566 U.S. 560 (2012) means document-translation cost is not taxable under 28 U.S.C. § 1920(6).
- [La preuve enregistrée en français](https://lexoral.org/preuve-enregistree/): version française.
- [What paragraph 530.1(g) requires](https://lexoral.org/section-530/): Criminal Code s. 530 gives an accused a trial in their own official language; paragraph 530.1(g) requires the record to include a transcript of everything said in the language it was said, a transcript of any interpretation into the other official language, and documentary evidence in the language it was tendered — three transcripts, not one. R. v. Munkonda, 2015 ONCA 309 (committal quashed, costs awarded; the court reporter was unilingual anglophone). Also covers Constitution Act, 1867 s. 133, Official Languages Act s. 14, and Courts of Justice Act (Ontario) s. 126(1).
- [Ce qu'exige l'alinéa 530.1g)](https://lexoral.org/article-530/): version française.
- [Frequently asked questions](https://lexoral.org/faq/): twenty-one answers grouped into what ends up in the record, attestation and admissibility, method, engaging us, confidentiality.
- [Questions fréquentes](https://lexoral.org/faq-fr/): version française.
- [Privacy Policy](https://lexoral.org/privacy/) · [Politique de confidentialité](https://lexoral.org/privacy-fr/): Loi 25 and GDPR compliance detail.
- [Retention Policy](https://lexoral.org/retention/) · [Politique de conservation](https://lexoral.org/retention-fr/): file retention and deletion.
- [Specimen transcript (PDF)](https://lexoral.org/lexoral-specimen-transcript.pdf): two-page sample in the delivered format, fictional matter.
